n: A messenger of the Lord comes from Gilgal, Israel’s first camp in Canaan, and speaks with God’s own voice: “I brought you out of Egypt… I will never break my covenant with you.” God’s faithfulness is the starting point.

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak, “messenger”; the word can mean a heavenly or an earthly messenger.

f.w: I will never break my covenant

n: God had told them to make no treaties with the Canaanites and to tear down their altars. They disobeyed, and He asks them to think about why.
Because they disobeyed, God will stop driving the nations out. Those peoples will become thorns in Israel’s side, and their gods a trap.
The people cry aloud at the rebuke. Their sorrow is real, though the coming chapters show it did not last.

f.w: lifted up their voice, and wept

n: They name the place Bochim, “weepers,” and offer sacrifices. Tears are a beginning, but lasting change requires turning.
The narrator steps back to Joshua’s time, when each tribe went to claim its land. This repeats Joshua 24:28 to set up the pattern of the whole book.

f.w: when Joshua had let the people go

n: Israel stayed faithful while Joshua and the elders who had personally witnessed God’s miracles were alive.
Joshua, the servant of the Lord, dies at 110.
He is buried on his land at Timnath-heres. The name is spelled with the letters reversed from Timnath-serah in Joshua.

f.g: “Portion of the sun”; Joshua 24:30 has Timnath-serah, “extra portion.”

n: A whole new generation grows up that does not know the Lord or His works. Faith was not passed on — a warning to every family and congregation.
Here begins the cycle of Judges: Israel sins by worshiping Baal-gods.

f.g: Plural of Baal, “lord” or “master,” the Canaanite storm and fertility god in his many local forms.

f.w: did evil in the sight of the LORD

n: They abandon the God who rescued them from Egypt for the gods of their neighbors. Forgetting what God has done leads to forsaking Him.
Baal and Ashtaroth were the main Canaanite fertility gods, believed to bring rain and crops — a constant temptation for farmers.

f.g: Plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war.

n: Second stage of the cycle: God lets enemies plunder and defeat Israel. Removing His protection is itself a form of judgment.

f.g: Handed them over, like selling a slave.

n: Wherever they went, things went wrong, exactly as God had warned in the covenant.

f.w: as the LORD had sworn unto them

n: Third stage: God raises up “judges,” deliverers who rescue Israel. These were more like military champions and leaders than courtroom judges.

f.g: Hebrew shophetim: leaders who “set things right,” delivering and governing.

n: Even so, Israel kept falling back into idolatry. Scripture often calls idolatry “whoring” because it betrays a covenant like marriage.

f.w: went a whoring after other gods
f.g: Spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to the covenant God as to a spouse.

n: God was with each judge, moved with compassion by Israel’s groaning under oppression. “Repented” here means He was moved to pity and changed course — not that He had sinned.

f.g: The Lord was moved with compassion; JST often clarifies passages that speak of God repenting.

n: When the judge died, Israel went back to idols and got even worse. The cycle is really a downward spiral.

f.w: corrupted themselves more than their fathers

n: God declares that Israel has broken His covenant and ignored His voice.
So He will no longer drive out the nations left after Joshua’s death.

f.w: I also will not henceforth drive out

n: The remaining nations become a test: will Israel keep the Lord’s way when temptation is close at hand? Mortality itself is such a test.
So God left those nations in the land, not rushing their removal, even in Joshua’s day.
